In PyCharm, press Ctrl + Q and click the NexoNest tag, such as #Curve.ClosestPoint. It opens that exact section here. Go beyond the signature with geometric explanations, worked examples, common mistakes, and 25 concept lessons. Overloads share one member section.

How to read this reference

Authored lessons explain geometric concepts and pitfalls. Other entries show the API-derived summary and signatures. Coverage is a partial Python view of RhinoCommon; supporting .NET types, null results, collection behavior, and runtime overload selection may need additional handling. Collection outputs use Sequence or Mapping abstractions rather than promising Python lists or dictionaries.

Examples target Rhino 8 Python and use geometry in memory. Stubs do not execute geometry or install Rhino. Model units, tolerances, validity, and success flags remain part of your algorithm's contract.

API summaries originate in RhinoCommon XML documentation. Rhino and RhinoCommon are products of Robert McNeel & Associates. NexoRhino is an independent NexoNest project. See the software terms.

AngularDimension.Create

def Create(dimStyle: DimensionStyle, line1: Line, pointOnLine1: Point3d, line2: Line, pointOnLine2: Point3d, pointOnAngularDimensionArc: Point3d, bSetExtensionPoints: bool) -> AngularDimension
def Create(dimStyle: DimensionStyle, plane: Plane, horizontal: Vector3d, centerpoint: Point3d, defpoint1: Point3d, defpoint2: Point3d, dimlinepoint: Point3d) -> AngularDimension
def Create(dimStyle: DimensionStyle, plane: Plane, horizontal: Vector3d, extpoint1: Point3d, extpoint2: Point3d, dirpoint1: Point3d, dirpoint2: Point3d, dimlinepoint: Point3d) -> AngularDimension
def Create(styleId: Any, plane: Plane, extpoint1: Point3d, extpoint2: Point3d, dirpoint1: Point3d, dirpoint2: Point3d, dimlinepoint: Point3d) -> AngularDimension

API summary

The angle between the lines is dimensioned. If the lines intersect in a single point, that point is used as the center of the angular dimension arc.In this case, there are eight possible angles to dimension.The pointOnAngularDimensionArc and pointOnLine parameters are used to select the correct angle to dimension. If a pointOnLine parameter is not set, the corresponding line's midpoint is used. If the lines are colinear, the point on the line closest to pointOnAngularDimensionArc is the center of the angular dimension arc.

Arc

32 members
#Arcanglescurves

NexoNest explanation

An arc is a portion of a circle, represented by a plane, radius, and angular interval. Angles are in radians; a curve parameter is not necessarily an angle or a distance.

An arc has constant curvature over a finite angular interval. An ArcCurve wrapper exposes the Curve API and its own parameter domain.

Separate a path's shape from its representation

A line, a circular arc, a polyline, and a NURBS curve can all be paths, but they encode shape differently. An exact analytic circle has angular evaluation; a Curve wrapper supplies a general parameter domain. Converting representation does not guarantee parameter identity.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

Arc.PointAt

def PointAt(self, t: float) -> Point3d

NexoNest explanation

Arc.PointAt evaluates an angle in radians within AngleDomain. The start angle need not be zero.

Distinguish absolute angle from angular distance measured from the start. Curve wrappers can use an entirely different parameter domain.

Angles need a unit, reference, and orientation

An angle is incomplete without its unit and orientation convention. Radians relate angular travel to circle length by s=r*angle. A numeric value of 90 is a quarter-turn in degrees but a very different rotation in radians.

AreaMassProperties

26 members
#AreaMassPropertiesmeasurement

NexoNest explanation

Area has squared model units; an area centroid is an area-weighted location. Open surfaces can have area without enclosing a volume.

Integrated area weighting differs from averaging vertices. Nonuniform tessellation makes unweighted sample averages particularly misleading.

Integrated measurements need the right weighting

Length, area, and volume have different units and weighting rules. A curve centroid is length-weighted, a surface centroid is area-weighted, and a solid centroid is volume-weighted. Averaging control points or tessellation vertices generally gives a different quantity.

NexoNest explanation

Area integration can fail and carries numerical error estimates. Check the result object before reading it.

Area has squared model units. The centroid is weighted by continuous area rather than by the number of sampled vertices.

When to use this

Measure continuous surface area or obtain an area-weighted centroid for a valid integration workflow.

Worked example · Vertex density does not change a plate centroid

  1. A uniform rectangular plate from (0,0) to (10,2) has area 20 and area centroid (5,1).
  2. Tessellating its left half more densely adds vertices there without changing the plate area or the physical centroid.
  3. An unweighted average of vertices can shift left. Area-weighted integration preserves the intended geometric quantity, subject to numerical accuracy.

Common mistakes

  • Replacing an integrated centroid with an average of control points or mesh vertices.
  • Reading a failed integration result without checking it.

Related lessons: #AreaMassProperties · #VolumeMassProperties.Compute · #LengthMassProperties

Integrated measurements need the right weighting

Length, area, and volume have different units and weighting rules. A curve centroid is length-weighted, a surface centroid is area-weighted, and a solid centroid is volume-weighted. Averaging control points or tessellation vertices generally gives a different quantity.

BezierCurve

23 members
#BezierCurvenurbs

NexoNest explanation

A Bezier curve uses a polynomial or rational control polygon over one span. Interior control points generally do not lie on the curve.

Endpoint control points locate the endpoints; neighboring control points influence endpoint tangents. The control polygon is an editing structure, not a sampled curve.

Read a NURBS control structure without confusing it with the shape

A NURBS curve combines a degree, control locations, weights, and knot values. Basis functions blend the control locations; the controls are editing handles, not generally samples on the curve. A quadratic Bezier with controls (0,0), (1,2), (2,0) evaluates to (1,1) at its midpoint rather than passing through the middle control.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

BezierSurface

19 members
#BezierSurfacenurbs

NexoNest explanation

A Bezier surface uses a tensor-product control net. The net is not a mesh of points on the evaluated surface.

Parameter spacing follows basis functions rather than physical distance. Geometry-aware sampling is needed when spatial regularity matters.

Read a NURBS control structure without confusing it with the shape

A NURBS curve combines a degree, control locations, weights, and knot values. Basis functions blend the control locations; the controls are editing handles, not generally samples on the curve. A quadratic Bezier with controls (0,0), (1,2), (2,0) evaluates to (1,1) at its midpoint rather than passing through the middle control.

A quadratic Bezier with controls (0,0), (1,2), (2,0) evaluates to (1,1) at its midpoint rather than passing through the middle control.

BoundingBox

25 members
#BoundingBoxmutationspatial-indextransforms

NexoNest explanation

An axis-aligned box bounds geometry in a coordinate frame. Overlapping boxes are useful for broad-phase rejection, but do not prove the enclosed objects intersect.

Use inexpensive bounds to reject distant candidates before exact tests. Coordinate-frame choice affects how tight the enclosure can be.

Use an index to find candidates, then test geometry

A spatial index organizes inexpensive proxies such as points and bounding boxes. It reduces how many expensive geometry comparisons you need, but a proxy hit does not generally prove an exact intersection or a requested distance condition.

BoundingBox.Transform

def Transform(self, xform: Transform) -> bool

NexoNest explanation

Transforming a box produces an axis-aligned enclosure of transformed corners, which can exceed an oriented enclosure.

Repeatedly transforming axis-aligned bounds can accumulate empty space. Retain a Box and its frame when orientation matters.

Reason about transformation order with a known point

Transform composition is ordered. With RhinoCommon's point transformation convention, A*B applies B first and then A. Scaling x=1 by two and then translating by ten gives x=12; translating first and scaling afterward gives x=22.

BoundingBox.Union

BoundingBox.Union(a: BoundingBox, b: BoundingBox) -> BoundingBox
BoundingBox.Union(box: BoundingBox, point: Point3d) -> BoundingBox
<instance>.Union(a: BoundingBox, b: BoundingBox) -> BoundingBox
<instance>.Union(box: BoundingBox, point: Point3d) -> BoundingBox
<instance>.Union(other: BoundingBox) -> None
<instance>.Union(point: Point3d) -> None

NexoNest explanation

Instance Union modifies a box and returns None. Static Union returns a new BoundingBox.

The result is an axis-aligned enclosure, not a Boolean solid union. Empty space between disjoint input boxes remains inside that enclosure.

When to use this

Build a conservative axis-aligned enclosure for spatial indexing, view fitting, or broad-phase rejection.

Worked example · An enclosure is not a solid Boolean

  1. Let box A span coordinates 0 through 1 on every axis, and box B span 2 through 3.
  2. The bounding union spans 0 through 3 on every axis, including empty space between the two boxes.
  3. Static Union returns a new box. Instance Union updates its receiver and returns None; choose the form according to ownership.

Rhino 8 Python example · geometry in memory

import Rhino.Geometry as rg
a = rg.BoundingBox(rg.Point3d(0, 0, 0), rg.Point3d(1, 1, 1))
b = rg.BoundingBox(rg.Point3d(2, 2, 2), rg.Point3d(3, 3, 3))
combined = rg.BoundingBox.Union(a, b)
assert abs(combined.Max.X - 3) < 1e-9

Common mistakes

  • Assigning the None result of instance Union back to the box variable.
  • Treating overlap of bounding enclosures as proof of a geometric intersection.

Related lessons: #BoundingBox.Contains · #BoundingBox.Transform · #RTree.Search

A geometry method may change its receiver

An operation can return new geometry, modify an existing object, or do both through outputs. Its name alone does not establish ownership. A void return becomes None in Python; assigning that result back to your geometry variable can discard your reference.

Box

25 members
#Boxframesparameters

NexoNest explanation

A Box combines a plane and three intervals, allowing orientation relative to world axes.

Its BoundingBox is an axis-aligned enclosure and can be much larger. Preserve the local frame for orientation-dependent packing and dimensions.

A local frame is a small coordinate system

A plane frame places an origin and three oriented axes in space. With orthonormal axes, P=O+u*X+v*Y+w*Z reconstructs a position from local coordinates. Setting w=0 projects the position onto the plane and loses its normal offset.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

Box.PointAt

def PointAt(self, x: float, y: float, z: float) -> Point3d

NexoNest explanation

Box.PointAt uses normalized coordinates along its intervals, evaluated in the local frame.

Coordinates from zero to one span each interval. They are not model distances measured along the plane axes.

Parameters are addresses, not distances

Think of C(t) as an address-to-position map. Its domain tells you which addresses are available; the derivative tells you how quickly position changes as the address changes. Changing the domain can change those numbers without changing the curve's shape.

Brep

129 members
#Brepdistancetolerancetopology

NexoNest explanation

A boundary representation combines geometric surfaces and curves with face, edge, and vertex topology. A valid Brep is not necessarily a closed solid.

Geometry describes shape; topology describes connections. Matching edge coordinates do not necessarily mean two faces share one topological edge.

Connectivity is information beyond coordinates

Geometry describes shapes; topology records how pieces are connected and oriented. Two edges can have matching coordinates without being the same topological edge. A Brep combines surfaces with faces, loops, trims, edges, and vertices to represent these relationships.

Brep.IsSurface

def IsSurface(self) -> bool

API summary

Returns true if the Brep has a single face and that face is geometrically the same as the underlying surface. I.e., the face has trivial trimming. In this case, the surface is the first face surface. The flag Brep.Faces[0].OrientationIsReversed records the correspondence between the surface's natural parametric orientation and the orientation of the Brep. trivial trimming here means that there is only one loop curve in the brep and that loop curve is the same as the underlying surface boundary.

Brep.ClosestPoint

def ClosestPoint(self, testPoint: Point3d) -> Point3d
def ClosestPoint(self, testPoint: Point3d, maximumDistance: float) -> tuple[bool, Point3d, ComponentIndex, float, float, Vector3d]

NexoNest explanation

The nearest point can belong to a face, edge, or vertex. Overloads return different additional information.

Interpret returned parameters with the component type. Edge parameters cannot be blindly interpreted as surface UV coordinates.

Choose the right notion of closeness

Straight-line distance, travel along a curve, and travel constrained to a surface answer different questions. Endpoints of a loop can coincide while traveling between them around the loop takes substantial length. Use the metric that matches the intended movement or clearance.

Brep.JoinBreps

def JoinBreps(brepsToJoin: Iterable[Brep], tolerance: float) -> Sequence[Brep]
def JoinBreps(brepsToJoin: Iterable[Brep], tolerance: float, angleTolerance: float) -> Sequence[Brep] | tuple[Sequence[Brep], Sequence[Sequence[int]]]

NexoNest explanation

Joining merges compatible boundaries within tolerance. It does not guarantee a closed or valid result.

Inspect naked edges. Raising tolerance can conceal mismatches and should follow a deliberate modeling accuracy policy.

A tolerance is a modeling policy, not a repair button

A distance tolerance has physical scale; an angular tolerance has a different unit and purpose. A 0.01 tolerance can mean ten millimeters in a meter-based dataset or a hundredth of a millimeter in a millimeter-based dataset. Choose it after unit conversion and according to the smallest feature that should remain distinct.

Brep.Trim

def Trim(self, cutter: Brep, intersectionTolerance: float) -> Sequence[Brep]
def Trim(self, cutter: Plane, intersectionTolerance: float) -> Sequence[Brep]

API summary

Trims a brep with an oriented cutter. The parts of the brep that lie inside (opposite the normal) of the cutter are retained while the parts to the outside (in the direction of the normal) are discarded. If the Cutter is closed, then a connected component of the Brep that does not intersect the cutter is kept if and only if it is contained in the inside of cutter. That is the region bounded by cutter opposite from the normal of cutter, If cutter is not closed all these components are kept.

BrepFace.DuplicateSurface

def DuplicateSurface(self) -> Surface

NexoNest explanation

The duplicated underlying surface does not retain the face's trimming loops.

Use DuplicateFace to preserve trims. The untrimmed surface can extend through holes and beyond the visible face boundary.

Understand the underlying surface and the retained region

A parametric surface maps (u,v) to a spatial point. Local derivatives determine how a small UV step stretches or turns in 3D. A uniform parameter grid can therefore become very uneven spatially, especially near poles or degenerate parameter regions.

16 members
#BrepTrimtopology

NexoNest explanation

A trim is a curve in face parameter space, connected to Brep topology.

Its parameterization can differ from the corresponding 3D edge. Use correspondence methods instead of equating their parameters.

Connectivity is information beyond coordinates

Geometry describes shapes; topology records how pieces are connected and oriented. Two edges can have matching coordinates without being the same topological edge. A Brep combines surfaces with faces, loops, trims, edges, and vertices to represent these relationships.

BrepVertex.Tolerance

def Tolerance(self) -> float

API summary

Accuracy of vertex point, either >=0.0 or Rhino.RhinoMath.UnsetValue. A value of Rhino.RhinoMath.UnsetValue indicates that the tolerance should be computed. A value of 0.0 indicates that the distance from the vertex to any applicable edge or trim end is <= Rhino.RhinoMath.ZeroTolerance. If an edge begins or ends at this vertex, then the distance from the vertex's 3d point to the appropriate end of the edge's 3d curve must be <= this tolerance. If a trim begins or ends at this vertex, then the distance from the vertex's 3d point to the 3d point on the surface obtained by evaluating the surface at the appropriate end of the trimming curve must be <= this tolerance.

Circle

26 members
#Circleanglescurvesfittingnurbsparametersvectors

NexoNest explanation

A circle uses a plane and positive radius. Its evaluation parameter is an angle in radians.

PointAt(0) lies along the plane's X axis. Increasing angles rotate toward Y; conversion to a Curve introduces that curve's own domain.

Separate a path's shape from its representation

A line, a circular arc, a polyline, and a NURBS curve can all be paths, but they encode shape differently. An exact analytic circle has angular evaluation; a Curve wrapper supplies a general parameter domain. Converting representation does not guarantee parameter identity.

Circle.ClosestParameter

def ClosestParameter(self, testPoint: Point3d) -> tuple[bool, float]

NexoNest explanation

Python returns (success, angle), not a bare float. Check success before calling PointAt(angle).

A point on the normal axis through the center does not determine a unique closest angular direction. Do not rely on a particular angle in that case.

When to use this

Find an angular reference for a circular feature, radial placement, or a point that should lie on an exact analytic circle.

Worked example · Projection onto a radius-five circle

  1. Take a circle centered at the origin in WorldXY with radius 5 and test point (7,2,0).
  2. The nearest angular direction is atan2(2,7). Python returns the success flag together with that angle, not just one number.
  3. The projected point is (35/sqrt(53),10/sqrt(53),0). Its distance from the center is 5; its distance from the test point is sqrt(53)-5.
  4. Evaluate circle.PointAt(angle) only after success. If you convert the circle to a Curve, do not reuse that angle without checking the new curve parameterization.

Rhino 8 Python example · geometry in memory

import Rhino.Geometry as rg
circle = rg.Circle(5.0)
ok, angle = circle.ClosestParameter(rg.Point3d(7, 2, 0))
if not ok:
    raise ValueError("Projection failed")
point = circle.PointAt(angle)

Common mistakes

  • Unpacking the result as a bare float.
  • Passing degrees to an angular evaluation that expects radians.
  • Expecting a unique angular answer for a point on the normal axis through the center.

Related lessons: #Circle.PointAt · #Circle.ToNurbsCurve · #Curve.ClosestPoint

Parameters are addresses, not distances

Think of C(t) as an address-to-position map. Its domain tells you which addresses are available; the derivative tells you how quickly position changes as the address changes. Changing the domain can change those numbers without changing the curve's shape.

Evaluates whether or not this circle is co-planar with a given plane.

Geometry behind this class

A circle uses a plane and positive radius. Its evaluation parameter is an angle in radians.

Separate a path's shape from its representation

A line, a circular arc, a polyline, and a NURBS curve can all be paths, but they encode shape differently. An exact analytic circle has angular evaluation; a Curve wrapper supplies a general parameter domain. Converting representation does not guarantee parameter identity.

Circle.PointAt

def PointAt(self, t: float) -> Point3d

NexoNest explanation

Circle.PointAt evaluates an angle in radians. On a fixed circle, equal angular increments give equal arc-length increments.

This special relationship does not hold for arbitrary Curve parameters. An ArcCurve representing the circle can have a different domain.

Angles need a unit, reference, and orientation

An angle is incomplete without its unit and orientation convention. Radians relate angular travel to circle length by s=r*angle. A numeric value of 90 is a quarter-turn in degrees but a very different rotation in radians.

Circle.TangentAt

def TangentAt(self, t: float) -> Vector3d

NexoNest explanation

The tangent follows increasing angle and lies in the circle plane, perpendicular to the radius.

Orientation follows the circle's plane. A tangent alone does not determine a complete spatial frame.

Use vector operations as geometric predicates

A dot product tests directional alignment and supports projection. For vectors a and b it equals |a|*|b|*cos(angle); for unit vectors it is just the cosine. A near-zero value suggests perpendicularity only after accounting for scale and tolerance.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

Permanent link · Official RhinoCommon reference

Circle.ToNurbsCurve

def ToNurbsCurve(self) -> NurbsCurve
def ToNurbsCurve(self, degree: int, cvCount: int) -> NurbsCurve

NexoNest explanation

Rational NURBS can represent a circle exactly. Rational weights enable that exact conic representation.

Exact shape does not imply identical parameterization. Use the returned curve's domain instead of reusing circle angles as NURBS parameters.

Rhino 8 Python example · geometry in memory

import Rhino.Geometry as rg
curve = rg.Circle(5.0).ToNurbsCurve()
assert curve is not None and curve.IsClosed

Read a NURBS control structure without confusing it with the shape

A NURBS curve combines a degree, control locations, weights, and knot values. Basis functions blend the control locations; the controls are editing handles, not generally samples on the curve. A quadratic Bezier with controls (0,0), (1,2), (2,0) evaluates to (1,1) at its midpoint rather than passing through the middle control.

Circle.TryFitCircleToPoints

def TryFitCircleToPoints(points: Iterable[Point3d]) -> tuple[bool, Circle]

NexoNest explanation

A fitted circle approximates samples. Success does not mean every sample lies exactly on the circle.

Measure residuals and inspect sample distribution. Nearly collinear or clustered points can make the radius estimate unstable.

Passing through data and explaining data are different goals

Interpolation aims to pass through samples; approximation allows residuals in exchange for another objective such as smoothness or fewer controls. Neither operation removes the need to inspect noisy or unevenly distributed input data.

ClippingPlaneSurface

10 members
#ClippingPlaneSurfacesurfaces

API summary

Represents a planar surface that is used as clipping plane in viewports. A clipping plane object maintains a list of viewports that it clips against.

Understand the underlying surface and the retained region

A parametric surface maps (u,v) to a spatial point. Local derivatives determine how a small UV step stretches or turns in 3D. A uniform parameter grid can therefore become very uneven spatially, especially near poles or degenerate parameter regions.

ComponentIndex

9 members
#ComponentIndextopology

NexoNest explanation

A component reference combines subobject kind and an index within its owner.

Topology changes can invalidate saved indices. Retain owner identity and revision when persistent correspondence matters.

Connectivity is information beyond coordinates

Geometry describes shapes; topology records how pieces are connected and oriented. Two edges can have matching coordinates without being the same topological edge. A Brep combines surfaces with faces, loops, trims, edges, and vertices to represent these relationships.

Cone

15 members
#Conesurfaces

NexoNest explanation

A cone narrows to an apex, where regular surface parameterization becomes singular.

Normals and tangent directions at the apex need special handling. Uniform parameter sampling can become spatially uneven near it.

Understand the underlying surface and the retained region

A parametric surface maps (u,v) to a spatial point. Local derivatives determine how a small UV step stretches or turns in 3D. A uniform parameter grid can therefore become very uneven spatially, especially near poles or degenerate parameter regions.

ControlPoint

9 members
#ControlPointnurbs

NexoNest explanation

A NURBS control point combines a Euclidean location and rational weight. It usually is not a point on the geometry.

Changing weight alters the basis contribution without moving the stored location. Preserve weights when exchanging rational curves and surfaces.

Read a NURBS control structure without confusing it with the shape

A NURBS curve combines a degree, control locations, weights, and knot values. Basis functions blend the control locations; the controls are editing handles, not generally samples on the curve. A quadratic Bezier with controls (0,0), (1,2), (2,0) evaluates to (1,1) at its midpoint rather than passing through the middle control.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

Curve

138 members
#Curvecalculuscurvesdistancefittingframesmeasurementmutationnurbsparametersprojectionsamplingtolerancetopologyvectors

NexoNest explanation

A parametric curve maps one parameter t to a point in space. Equal parameter steps generally do not produce equal distances. Use length-based sampling when physical spacing matters.

Parameter speed is the magnitude of the derivative with respect to t. Changing the domain can change speed without changing the geometric path.

Parameters are addresses, not distances

Think of C(t) as an address-to-position map. Its domain tells you which addresses are available; the derivative tells you how quickly position changes as the address changes. Changing the domain can change those numbers without changing the curve's shape.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

Geometry describes shapes; topology records how pieces are connected and oriented. Two edges can have matching coordinates without being the same topological edge. A Brep combines surfaces with faces, loops, trims, edges, and vertices to represent these relationships.

Permanent link · Official RhinoCommon reference

Curve.ClosestPoint

def ClosestPoint(self, testPoint: Point3d) -> tuple[bool, float]
def ClosestPoint(self, testPoint: Point3d, maximumDistance: float) -> tuple[bool, float]

NexoNest explanation

The result is a curve parameter, not a distance. Evaluate PointAt(t) to obtain the projected point, and check success before using t.

After successful projection, evaluate PointAt(t) and measure the distance. The maximum-distance overload can reject distant candidates; a parameter alone is not a distance.

When to use this

Use this to attach a measured point to a path, find a curve location for a connector, or measure clearance after evaluating the projection. Use length methods instead when the question is how far to travel along the path.

Worked example · A parameter that is neither distance nor a fraction

  1. Consider a straight curve from (0,0,0) to (10,0,0), explicitly reparameterized to Domain=[10,20].
  2. For the test point (3,4,0), the closest location is (3,0,0). On this chosen linear parameterization its parameter is t=13.
  3. The straight-line distance from the test point is 4, not 13. The normalized domain coordinate is 0.3, another different quantity.
  4. Check success, evaluate curve.PointAt(t), then measure testPoint.DistanceTo(projected). Keep t only as a reference to this curve and its current parameterization.

Rhino 8 Python example · geometry in memory

import Rhino.Geometry as rg
curve = rg.ArcCurve(rg.Circle(5.0))
ok, t = curve.ClosestPoint(rg.Point3d(7, 2, 0))
if not ok:
    raise ValueError("Projection failed")
projected = curve.PointAt(t)

Common mistakes

  • Treating t as a length or assuming it is between zero and one.
  • Reusing a saved t after reversing, rebuilding, or replacing the curve without checking correspondence.
  • Ignoring the success flag from the maximum-distance overload.

Related lessons: #Curve.PointAt · #Curve.LengthParameter · #Curve.PointAtNormalizedLength

Choose the right notion of closeness

Straight-line distance, travel along a curve, and travel constrained to a surface answer different questions. Endpoints of a loop can coincide while traveling between them around the loop takes substantial length. Use the metric that matches the intended movement or clearance.

Read a NURBS control structure without confusing it with the shape

A NURBS curve combines a degree, control locations, weights, and knot values. Basis functions blend the control locations; the controls are editing handles, not generally samples on the curve. Passing through data and explaining data are different goals

Interpolation aims to pass through samples; approximation allows residuals in exchange for another objective such as smoothness or fewer controls. Neither operation removes the need to inspect noisy or unevenly distributed input data.

Curve.CurvatureAt

def CurvatureAt(self, t: float) -> Vector3d

NexoNest explanation

Curvature measures how rapidly the tangent changes with arc length. Its magnitude has inverse-length units; a circle of radius r has curvature magnitude 1/r.

Nonzero curvature has a reciprocal local radius. Curvature vanishes on straight regions and may not have one smooth value at a discontinuity.

Derivatives connect parameters to geometric behavior

A first derivative describes change per unit of parameter, so its magnitude depends on parameterization. A unit tangent retains direction while removing that scale. Curvature instead measures tangent change per unit of arc length; its units are inverse length.

Curve.FrameAt

def FrameAt(self, t: float) -> tuple[bool, Plane]

NexoNest explanation

Curve-frame orientation depends on tangent and curvature. Straight and singular regions can make it unstable.

For section placement, compare perpendicular-frame methods and inspect frame rotation between samples. Closed seams need an explicit continuity policy.

A local frame is a small coordinate system

A plane frame places an origin and three oriented axes in space. With orthonormal axes, P=O+u*X+v*Y+w*Z reconstructs a position from local coordinates. Setting w=0 projects the position onto the plane and loses its normal offset.

NexoNest explanation

Arc length measures distance along the curve in model units. A parameter-domain length is generally a different quantity.

Numerical integration and tolerance affect estimates. A closed curve can have coincident endpoints while retaining substantial arc length.

Integrated measurements need the right weighting

Length, area, and volume have different units and weighting rules. A curve centroid is length-weighted, a surface centroid is area-weighted, and a solid centroid is volume-weighted. Averaging control points or tessellation vertices generally gives a different quantity.

NexoNest explanation

Joining connects compatible endpoints within tolerance. It does not guarantee one result or a closed curve.

Inspect result count and closure. Excessive tolerance can connect unintended endpoints or conceal meaningful gaps.

A tolerance is a modeling policy, not a repair button

A distance tolerance has physical scale; an angular tolerance has a different unit and purpose. A 0.01 tolerance can mean ten millimeters in a meter-based dataset or a hundredth of a millimeter in a millimeter-based dataset. Choose it after unit conversion and according to the smallest feature that should remain distinct.

One local frame does not guarantee a globally consistent sequence. Inflections, sampling direction, and closed seams can introduce apparent twists.

A local frame is a small coordinate system

A plane frame places an origin and three oriented axes in space. With orthonormal axes, P=O+u*X+v*Y+w*Z reconstructs a position from local coordinates. Setting w=0 projects the position onto the plane and loses its normal offset.

Curve.PointAt

def PointAt(self, t: float) -> Point3d

NexoNest explanation

Evaluate t in the curve's Domain. A parameter is not generally a distance or normalized fraction.

Use length-to-parameter conversion for measured spacing. Query the domain before assuming a range such as [0,1].

When to use this

Use a parameter already associated with this curve, such as an output from ClosestPoint, Split, or a length-to-parameter conversion.

Worked example · Why a parameter midpoint may not be a length midpoint

  1. As a mathematical example, let C(t)=(t*t,0,0) on [0,1]. The set of points is a straight unit segment, but its parameter speed is nonuniform.
  2. At t=0.5 the point is (0.25,0,0), so the parameter midpoint reaches only a quarter of the path length.
  3. Half the arc length is at (0.5,0,0), corresponding to t=sqrt(0.5). This is why physical spacing needs length-based methods.

Common mistakes

  • Normalizing a domain and assuming it also normalizes speed.
  • Using a parameter from a different representation of the same geometric shape.

Related lessons: #Curve.PointAtNormalizedLength · #Interval.ParameterAt · #Curve.DerivativeAt

Parameters are addresses, not distances

Think of C(t) as an address-to-position map. Its domain tells you which addresses are available; the derivative tells you how quickly position changes as the address changes. Changing the domain can change those numbers without changing the curve's shape.

Curve.PointAtNormalizedLength

def PointAtNormalizedLength(self, length: float) -> Point3d

NexoNest explanation

A normalized length fraction refers to arc length, not the curve's parameter interval.

The fraction 0.5 identifies the halfway point along a valid curve. A parameter-domain midpoint can be at a different location.

When to use this

Place repeated elements or query a fraction of travel along a path when geometric distance matters more than its internal parameter addresses.

Worked example · Travel spacing and chord spacing

  1. On a circle of radius r, a quarter of total arc length travels pi*r/2 along the circle.
  2. The straight chord joining those quarter-turn endpoints has length r*sqrt(2), which is different.
  3. Length fractions control travel along the curve. If a design requires straight connector lengths, measure the resulting chords separately.

Rhino 8 Python example · geometry in memory

import Rhino.Geometry as rg
curve = rg.LineCurve(rg.Point3d(0, 0, 0), rg.Point3d(10, 0, 0))
midpoint = curve.PointAtNormalizedLength(0.5)
assert abs(midpoint.X - 5) < 1e-9

Common mistakes

  • Calling equal arc-length samples equal straight-line separations on an arbitrary bent curve.
  • Duplicating the same seam location when sampling both fractions 0 and 1 on a closed curve.

Related lessons: #Curve.DivideByCount · #Curve.LengthParameter · #Point3d.DistanceTo

Sample according to the quantity you intend to preserve

Uniform parameter samples, equal arc-length samples, equal-area samples, and curvature-adaptive samples serve different purposes. Equal arc length along a bent curve does not imply equal straight-line separation between consecutive points.

Curve.Simplify

API summary

Returns a geometrically equivalent PolyCurve. The PolyCurve has the following properties 1. All the PolyCurve segments are LineCurve, PolylineCurve, ArcCurve, or NurbsCurve. 2. The NURBS Curves segments do not have fully multiple interior knots. 3. Rational NURBS curves do not have constant weights. 4. Any segment for which IsLinear() or IsArc() is true is a Line, Polyline segment, or an Arc. 5. Adjacent co-linear or co-circular segments are combined. 6. Segments that meet with G1-continuity have there ends tuned up so that they meet with G1-continuity to within machine precision.

A parametric curve maps one parameter t to a point in space. Equal parameter steps generally do not produce equal distances. Use length-based sampling when physical spacing matters.

Parameters are addresses, not distances

Think of C(t) as an address-to-position map. Its domain tells you which addresses are available; the derivative tells you how quickly position changes as the address changes. Changing the domain can change those numbers without changing the curve's shape.

Connectivity is information beyond coordinates

Curve.TangentAt

NexoNest explanation

The tangent describes the direction of increasing parameter. It is neither a position nor a curvature measurement.

Reversing the curve reverses traversal. At singular or discontinuous regions, a stable tangent may not be available.

Use vector operations as geometric predicates

A dot product tests directional alignment and supports projection. For vectors a and b it equals |a|*|b|*cos(angle); for unit vectors it is just the cosine. A near-zero value suggests perpendicularity only after accounting for scale and tolerance.

Cylinder

#Cylindersurfaces

NexoNest explanation

A cylinder combines a circular cross section and an axis; height limits determine its finite extent.

An analytic cylinder and a capped Brep solid are different representations. Inspect conversion options and closure when volume matters.

Understand the underlying surface and the retained region

A parametric surface maps (u,v) to a spatial point. Local derivatives determine how a small UV step stretches or turns in 3D. A uniform parameter grid can therefore become very uneven spatially, especially near poles or degenerate parameter regions.

Ellipse

10 members
#Ellipsecurves

NexoNest explanation

An ellipse is a planar conic with two principal radii. Its angular parameter is not proportional to arc length.

Equal angular steps travel different distances. Convert to a Curve and use length methods for uniform physical spacing.

Separate a path's shape from its representation

A line, a circular arc, a polyline, and a NURBS curve can all be paths, but they encode shape differently. An exact analytic circle has angular evaluation; a Curve wrapper supplies a general parameter domain. Converting representation does not guarantee parameter identity.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

Extrusion

33 members
#Extrusionsurfacestopology

NexoNest explanation

An extrusion stores profiles and a path compactly. Caps and inner profiles determine solid enclosure.

It can be more economical than a general Brep. Convert when topology is needed and verify IsSolid for volume-related tasks.

Understand the underlying surface and the retained region

A parametric surface maps (u,v) to a spatial point. Local derivatives determine how a small UV step stretches or turns in 3D. A uniform parameter grid can therefore become very uneven spatially, especially near poles or degenerate parameter regions.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

Geometry behind this class

An extrusion stores profiles and a path compactly. Caps and inner profiles determine solid enclosure.

Understand the underlying surface and the retained region

A parametric surface maps (u,v) to a spatial point. Local derivatives determine how a small UV step stretches or turns in 3D. A uniform parameter grid can therefore become very uneven spatially, especially near poles or degenerate parameter regions.

Extrusion.ToBrep

def ToBrep(self) -> Brep
def ToBrep(self, splitKinkyFaces: bool) -> Brep

NexoNest explanation

Conversion expands compact extrusion geometry into Brep faces and edges.

Component indices and identity can change. Recompute topology references instead of assuming a one-to-one index mapping.

Connectivity is information beyond coordinates

Geometry describes shapes; topology records how pieces are connected and oriented. Two edges can have matching coordinates without being the same topological edge. A Brep combines surfaces with faces, loops, trims, edges, and vertices to represent these relationships.

GeometryBase.DuplicateShallow

def DuplicateShallow(self) -> GeometryBase

API summary

Constructs a light copy of this object. By "light", it is meant that the same underlying data is used until something is done to attempt to change it. For example, you could have a shallow copy of a very heavy mesh object and the same underlying data will be used when doing things like inspecting the number of faces on the mesh. If you modify the location of one of the mesh vertices, the shallow copy will create a full duplicate of the underlying mesh data and the shallow copy will become a deep copy.

Hatch

15 members
#Hatchannotations

NexoNest explanation

A hatch combines planar boundaries and a display pattern. Pattern scale differs from boundary geometry.

Loops define filled regions and holes. Pattern appearance does not establish a connected surface or a solid.

Keep presentation separate from model geometry

A label, dimension, hatch, or text entity carries presentation choices as well as geometric placement. Font, display scale, reference plane, and formatting can change appearance without changing the geometric quantity being described.

HiddenLineDrawingParameters.SetViewport

def SetViewport(self, viewport: RhinoViewport) -> None
def SetViewport(self, viewport: ViewportInfo) -> None

API summary

Set the viewport for the hidden line drawing (HLD). The viewport supplies the projection that determines the visibility of curves, and the HLD coordinate system in which the resulting curves are represented. The HLD-coordinate system is a right handed system for 3-D model space, in which the 3rd coordinate direction is the projection direction. In particular the z-coordinate direction points from the scene toward the camera.

HiddenLineDrawingSegment.CurveSideFills

def CurveSideFills(self) -> Sequence[Any]

API summary

The SideFill fields are only valid for visible curves. With respect to the HiddenLineDrawing, the region to the left (or right respectively) of this curve is described by CurveSideFills[0] or CurveSideFills[1], respectively. If exactly one of these regions is empty this is a scene silhouette. If this region contains a surface it is either a surface which in 3-D is adjacent to this edge or it an surface that is further away from the camera, we call this a shadow surface. unknown is used for unset values and for projecting curves

Interval

29 members
#Intervalparameters

NexoNest explanation

An interval is an ordered numeric domain. Endpoints can increase, decrease, or coincide; domain length is not geometric arc length.

Preserve endpoint order when it encodes direction. A collapsed interval cannot support a meaningful inverse normalization.

Parameters are addresses, not distances

Think of C(t) as an address-to-position map. Its domain tells you which addresses are available; the derivative tells you how quickly position changes as the address changes. Changing the domain can change those numbers without changing the curve's shape.

Permanent link · Official RhinoCommon reference

Interval.ParameterAt

def ParameterAt(self, normalizedParameter: float) -> float

NexoNest explanation

Map a normalized coordinate s to T0 + s*(T1-T0). Values outside [0,1] extrapolate.

For a curve domain, s=0.5 gives its parameter midpoint. This is not generally the halfway point along the curve's arc length.

assert domain.ParameterAt(0.25) == 12.5

Parameters are addresses, not distances

Think of C(t) as an address-to-position map. Its domain tells you which addresses are available; the derivative tells you how quickly position changes as the address changes. Changing the domain can change those numbers without changing the curve's shape.

Interval.Reverse

def Reverse(self) -> None

LengthMassProperties

26 members
#LengthMassPropertiesmeasurement

NexoNest explanation

Length mass properties weight quantities continuously along a curve.

A length centroid differs from an unweighted average of sampled points, especially when sampling is uneven.

Integrated measurements need the right weighting

Length, area, and volume have different units and weighting rules. A curve centroid is length-weighted, a surface centroid is area-weighted, and a solid centroid is volume-weighted. Averaging control points or tessellation vertices generally gives a different quantity.

Light.SpotExponent

def SpotExponent(self) -> float

API summary

The spot exponent varies from 0.0 to 128.0 and provides an exponential interface for controlling the focus or concentration of a spotlight (like the OpenGL GL_SPOT_EXPONENT parameter). The spot exponent and hot spot parameters are linked; changing one will change the other. A hot spot setting of 0.0 corresponds to a spot exponent of 128. A hot spot setting of 1.0 corresponds to a spot exponent of 0.0.

Line

34 members
#Linecurvesdistanceinteropnurbsparameters

NexoNest explanation

A Line is a finite segment parameterized by From + t*Direction. Its segment corresponds to t in [0,1].

Parameters outside that interval lie on the infinite extension. A LineCurve has its own Curve domain, which need not use the same parameterization.

Separate a path's shape from its representation

A line, a circular arc, a polyline, and a NURBS curve can all be paths, but they encode shape differently. An exact analytic circle has angular evaluation; a Curve wrapper supplies a general parameter domain. Converting representation does not guarantee parameter identity.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

Line.ClosestParameter

def ClosestParameter(self, testPoint: Point3d) -> float

NexoNest explanation

The parameter is normalized along the segment and can lie outside [0,1].

For a valid nonzero line, PointAt(t) reconstructs the supporting-line projection. Clamp explicitly when the result must remain on the finite segment.

Parameters are addresses, not distances

Think of C(t) as an address-to-position map. Its domain tells you which addresses are available; the derivative tells you how quickly position changes as the address changes. Changing the domain can change those numbers without changing the curve's shape.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

Permanent link · Official RhinoCommon reference

Line.ClosestPoint

def ClosestPoint(self, testPoint: Point3d, limitToFiniteSegment: bool) -> Point3d

NexoNest explanation

limitToFiniteSegment controls whether projection is clamped to the segment endpoints.

Unconstrained projection can lie beyond an endpoint. Choose according to whether your algorithm models a bounded edge or its infinite supporting line.

Rhino 8 Python example · geometry in memory

import Rhino.Geometry as rg
line = rg.Line(rg.Point3d(0, 0, 0), rg.Point3d(10, 0, 0))
p = line.ClosestPoint(rg.Point3d(15, 2, 0), True)
assert abs(p.X - 10) < 1e-9

Choose the right notion of closeness

Straight-line distance, travel along a curve, and travel constrained to a surface answer different questions. Endpoints of a loop can coincide while traveling between them around the loop takes substantial length. Use the metric that matches the intended movement or clearance.

Line.ToNurbsCurve

def ToNurbsCurve(self) -> NurbsCurve

NexoNest explanation

Conversion preserves the straight shape while changing its representation to NurbsCurve.

Check parameter correspondence before reusing saved values on the converted curve. Identical shape does not imply identical parameterization.

Read a NURBS control structure without confusing it with the shape

A NURBS curve combines a degree, control locations, weights, and knot values. Basis functions blend the control locations; the controls are editing handles, not generally samples on the curve. A quadratic Bezier with controls (0,0), (1,2), (2,0) evaluates to (1,1) at its midpoint rather than passing through the middle control.

Line.TryCreateBetweenCurves

def TryCreateBetweenCurves(curve0: Curve, curve1: Curve, t0: float, t1: float, perpendicular0: bool, perpendicular1: bool) -> tuple[bool, float, float, Line]

NexoNest explanation

t0 and t1 are ref inputs. Python returns success, their updated values, and the resulting line.

The input parameters are initial guesses. Keep the updated parameters when later geometry must correspond to the solver's endpoints.

Read Python.NET results in Python terms

A .NET out parameter is an output, not normally a Python argument. Python.NET collects outputs with the non-void return value in declaration order. A ref parameter still needs an initial input and also contributes its updated value to the result.

Mesh

135 members
#Meshdistanceinteropmeshestopology

NexoNest explanation

A polygon mesh approximates shape with vertices and faces. Density alone does not ensure quality: topology, normals, degeneracy, and manifoldness also matter.

Interpolated normals can create visual smoothness without geometrically smooth faces. Assess connectivity and task-specific error rather than appearance alone.

A smooth-looking mesh may still have problematic geometry

A mesh represents shape through vertices and polygon connectivity. Interpolated shading normals can make flat facets appear smooth without improving geometric accuracy. Increasing polygon count also does not automatically repair disconnected, degenerate, or nonmanifold regions.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

Mesh.IsClosed

def IsClosed(self) -> bool

NexoNest explanation

A closed mesh has no open boundary according to its connectivity. This alone does not establish a suitable solid.

Check manifoldness, consistent orientation, degeneracies, and self-intersection as needed. Visually coincident vertices may still be disconnected.

Connectivity is information beyond coordinates

Geometry describes shapes; topology records how pieces are connected and oriented. Two edges can have matching coordinates without being the same topological edge. A Brep combines surfaces with faces, loops, trims, edges, and vertices to represent these relationships.

Mesh.Ngons

def Ngons(self) -> Any

API summary

Gets access to the mesh ngon list. Ngons represent groups of Faces (triangles + quads). Faces are used to tessellate an Ngon internally. When a triangle or quad is referenced in the Ngon list, it is no longer visualized and conceived as a single entity, but takes part of the Ngon. If you need to get access to both Ngons and the faces that are not referenced by Ngons, that is, all polygons that are visible in the mesh, then use the Rhino.Geometry.Mesh.GetNgonAndFacesEnumerable helper method.

Mesh.Check

def Check(self, textLog: Any, parameters: MeshCheckParameters) -> tuple[bool, MeshCheckParameters]

NexoNest explanation

The parameters argument is a ref input. Python returns the Boolean result and updated MeshCheckParameters.

A report covers specific checks rather than every application requirement. Inspect which conditions were tested and retain diagnostic output.

Read Python.NET results in Python terms

A .NET out parameter is an output, not normally a Python argument. Python.NET collects outputs with the non-void return value in declaration order. A ref parameter still needs an initial input and also contributes its updated value to the result.

Mesh.ClosestMeshPoint

def ClosestMeshPoint(self, testPoint: Point3d, maximumDistance: float) -> MeshPoint

NexoNest explanation

A MeshPoint retains face and local-coordinate correspondence as well as position.

This supports attribute interpolation. Stored face indices can become invalid after topology-changing edits.

Choose the right notion of closeness

Straight-line distance, travel along a curve, and travel constrained to a surface answer different questions. Endpoints of a loop can coincide while traveling between them around the loop takes substantial length. Use the metric that matches the intended movement or clearance.

Mesh.ComputeCurvatureApproximation

def ComputeCurvatureApproximation(self, type: int) -> tuple[bool, Sequence[float]]

API summary

Compute an approximation of the discrete curvatures of the mesh vertices, according to which type of curvature information is requested. This method will not yield meaningful values on nonmanifold vertices, and nan on naked vertices. For now, this method operates solely on the mesh topology (the fully welded mesh), but distribtes the result across all the ordinary vertices. This method is a const and thread-safe method and will leave the m_K array untouched. An integer indicating which curvature is desired. gaussian_curvature = 1, mean_curvature = 2, minimum unsigned radius of curvature = 3, maximum unsigned radius of curvature = 4 Resulting curvature array on success, null on failure. On success, the length of the array is the number of vertices.

API summary

Constructs a icospherical mesh. A mesh icosphere differs from a standard UV mesh sphere in that it's vertices are evenly distributed. A mesh icosphere starts from an icosahedron (a regular polyhedron with 20 equilateral triangles). It is then refined by splitting each triangle into 4 smaller triangles. This splitting can be done several times.

Mesh.HealNakedEdges

def HealNakedEdges(self, distance: float) -> bool

API summary

Attempts to "heal" naked edges in a mesh based on a given distance. First attempts to move vertices to neighboring vertices that are within that distance away. Then it finds edges that have a closest point to the vertex within the distance and splits the edge. When it finds one it splits the edge and makes two new edges using that point.

Mesh.RequireIterativeCleanup

def RequireIterativeCleanup(meshes: Iterable[Mesh], tolerance: float) -> bool

API summary

Analyzes some meshes, and determines if a pass of CreateFromIterativeCleanup would change the array. All available cleanup steps are used. Currently available cleanup steps are: - mending of single precision coincidence even though double precision vertices differ. - union of nearly identical vertices, irrespectively of their origin. - removal of t-joints along edges.

Mesh.SetCachedTextureCoordinatesFromMaterial

def SetCachedTextureCoordinatesFromMaterial(self, rhinoObject: Any, material: Any) -> None

API summary

Sets up cached texture coordinate set for each texture in the material. Textures in the Material define which mapping channels are used and the RhinoObject defines what texture mapping is used for each mapping channel. After this method is called all necessary texture coordinate sets are cached and correct texture coordinates for each texture can be fetched using GetCachedTextureCoordinates(RhinoObject rhinoObject, Rhino.DocObjects.Texture texture) If any texture coordinates are already cached they will not be re-computed.

Mesh.SetSurfaceParametersFromTextureCoordinates

API summary

MeshFace

18 members
#MeshFacemeshes

NexoNest explanation

A face stores vertex indices. Triangles and quads have different index relationships.

Indices belong to the owning mesh and can change after edits. A nonplanar quad's triangulation affects interpolation and measurements.

A smooth-looking mesh may still have problematic geometry

A mesh represents shape through vertices and polygon connectivity. Interpolated shading normals can make flat facets appear smooth without improving geometric accuracy. Increasing polygon count also does not automatically repair disconnected, degenerate, or nonmanifold regions.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

MeshingParameters.ClosedObjectPostProcess

def ClosedObjectPostProcess(self) -> bool

API summary

Gets or sets a value indicating whether or not to post process non-closed meshes that should be closed. If the Brep being meshed is closed, JaggedSeams = false, and ClosedObjectPostProcess = true, and the resulting mesh is not closed, then a post meshing process is applied to find and close gaps in the mesh. Typically the resulting mesh is not closed because the input Brep has a geometric flaw, like loops in trimming curve.

MeshNgon

11 members
#MeshNgonmeshes

NexoNest explanation

An ngon groups underlying faces under a polygonal boundary; it does not remove those faces.

Use face membership for calculations. Ngon count is not a replacement for the underlying computational triangle count.

A smooth-looking mesh may still have problematic geometry

A mesh represents shape through vertices and polygon connectivity. Interpolated shading normals can make flat facets appear smooth without improving geometric accuracy. Increasing polygon count also does not automatically repair disconnected, degenerate, or nonmanifold regions.

MeshPoint.T

def T(self) -> Sequence[float]

API summary

Barycentric quad coordinates for the point on the mesh face mesh.Faces[FaceIndex]. If the face is a triangle disregard T[3] (it should be set to 0.0). If the face is a quad and is split between vertices 0 and 2, then T[3] will be 0.0 when point is on the triangle defined by vi[0], vi[1], vi[2], and T[1] will be 0.0 when point is on the triangle defined by vi[0], vi[2], vi[3]. If the face is a quad and is split between vertices 1 and 3, then T[2] will be 0.0 when point is on the triangle defined by vi[0], vi[1], vi[3], and m_t[0] will be 0.0 when point is on the triangle defined by vi[1], vi[2], vi[3].

NurbsCurve

38 members
#NurbsCurvenurbs

NexoNest explanation

A NURBS curve combines control points, weights, degree, and knots. Control points generally do not lie on the curve. Degree and knot multiplicity affect smoothness.

Basis functions over knot spans determine shape. Moving a control point and constraining an evaluated point are different geometric operations.

Read a NURBS control structure without confusing it with the shape

A NURBS curve combines a degree, control locations, weights, and knot values. Basis functions blend the control locations; the controls are editing handles, not generally samples on the curve. A quadratic Bezier with controls (0,0), (1,2), (2,0) evaluates to (1,1) at its midpoint rather than passing through the middle control.

A quadratic Bezier with controls (0,0), (1,2), (2,0) evaluates to (1,1) at its midpoint rather than passing through the middle control.

NurbsCurve.IsRational

def IsRational(self) -> bool

NexoNest explanation

Rational NURBS allow nonunit weights and exact conic representation.

Equal weights can represent a nonrational shape within rational storage. The property describes representation; changing individual weights changes relative control influence.

NurbsCurve.Knots

def Knots(self) -> Any

NexoNest explanation

Knots divide parameter space. Repeated interior knots can reduce parametric continuity.

For ordinary interior multiplicity m and degree p, continuity is generally C^(p-m). Geometric continuity can be higher in special configurations.

NurbsCurve.Points

def Points(self) -> Any

NexoNest explanation

Control points influence a curve through basis functions. Most do not lie on the evaluated shape.

Control-point edits affect a neighborhood determined by knots and degree. Inspect PointAt results rather than relying on the control polygon alone.

When to use this

Edit the control structure or inspect how a curve is represented. Use evaluation methods to obtain samples on the actual curve.

Worked example · A middle control point is not a curve midpoint

  1. A quadratic Bezier is a simple NURBS case. Give it controls P0=(0,0), P1=(1,2), P2=(2,0) with equal weights.
  2. At t=0.5 its blending weights are 0.25, 0.5, 0.25. The resulting point is (1,1).
  3. The middle control is (1,2), so placing an element there does not place it on the curve. Evaluate the curve or solve a geometric constraint instead.

Common mistakes

  • Using the control polygon as if it were a sampled toolpath.
  • Assuming a control-point edit moves only one isolated point of the evaluated curve.

Related lessons: #Curve.PointAt · #Curve.CreateControlPointCurve · #Curve.CreateInterpolatedCurve

NurbsSurface

34 members
#NurbsSurfacenurbs

NexoNest explanation

A tensor-product NURBS surface uses a control net and two knot directions. Its rectangular parameter domain does not imply uniform distances on the surface.

The control net defines an underlying surface. Brep topology adds trimmed regions and holes that need not follow the rectangular net.

A quadratic Bezier with controls (0,0), (1,2), (2,0) evaluates to (1,1) at its midpoint rather than passing through the middle control.

Plane

38 members
#Planedistanceframesmutation

NexoNest explanation

A valid plane is an oriented frame with an origin and orthonormal axes. Its Z axis is the normal.

Projection into plane coordinates loses the normal offset. Retain signed distance separately when the original 3D point must be reconstructed.

A local frame is a small coordinate system

A plane frame places an origin and three oriented axes in space. With orthonormal axes, P=O+u*X+v*Y+w*Z reconstructs a position from local coordinates. Setting w=0 projects the position onto the plane and loses its normal offset.

Plane.ClosestParameter

def ClosestParameter(self, testPoint: Point3d) -> tuple[bool, float, float]

NexoNest explanation

Python returns (success, u, v). Check success before evaluating PointAt(u,v).

For a valid orthonormal plane, the local axes measure model distances. Unlike a general surface domain, this parameterization has a uniform metric.

When to use this

Map spatial measurements into a local planar layout, a fabrication sheet, or a section frame.

Worked example · Projection loses the normal coordinate

  1. In WorldXY, the point (2,3,7) projects to local coordinates (u,v)=(2,3).
  2. Plane.PointAt(2,3) reconstructs (2,3,0), not the original point. The missing normal offset is 7.
  3. To preserve the full position, also retain the signed normal coordinate and use the three-coordinate PointAt overload with the same frame.

Rhino 8 Python example · geometry in memory

import Rhino.Geometry as rg
plane = rg.Plane.WorldXY
ok, u, v = plane.ClosestParameter(rg.Point3d(2, 3, 7))
if not ok:
    raise ValueError("Projection failed")
projected = plane.PointAt(u, v)

Common mistakes

  • Treating a projected pair as a reversible conversion of the full 3D position.
  • Applying the numbers in a different plane frame.

Related lessons: #Plane.PointAt · #Plane.DistanceTo · #Transform.ChangeBasis

Geometry behind this class

A valid plane is an oriented frame with an origin and orthonormal axes. Its Z axis is the normal.

A local frame is a small coordinate system

A plane frame places an origin and three oriented axes in space. With orthonormal axes, P=O+u*X+v*Y+w*Z reconstructs a position from local coordinates. Setting w=0 projects the position onto the plane and loses its normal offset.

Plane.DistanceTo

def DistanceTo(self, bbox: BoundingBox) -> tuple[bool, float, float]
def DistanceTo(self, testPoint: Point3d) -> float

NexoNest explanation

The point overload returns signed distance. Its sign depends on the plane normal.

Reversing the normal changes the sign without changing the plane's point set. Use absolute distance for orientation-independent proximity.

Choose the right notion of closeness

Straight-line distance, travel along a curve, and travel constrained to a surface answer different questions. Endpoints of a loop can coincide while traveling between them around the loop takes substantial length. Use the metric that matches the intended movement or clearance.

Plane.Flip

def Flip(self) -> None

NexoNest explanation

Flip exchanges X and Y axes and reverses orientation. It changes the plane and returns None.

The same geometric plane can have opposite normals. Orientation affects signed distance and apparent winding of planar curves.

Rhino 8 Python example · geometry in memory

import Rhino.Geometry as rg
plane = rg.Plane(rg.Plane.WorldXY)
plane.Flip()
assert plane.Normal.Z < 0

A geometry method may change its receiver

An operation can return new geometry, modify an existing object, or do both through outputs. Its name alone does not establish ownership. A void return becomes None in Python; assigning that result back to your geometry variable can discard your reference.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

API summary

Enumerates all possible outcomes of a Least-Squares plane fitting operation.

Turn a signature into a geometric decision

Before choosing a method, state the geometric question: do you need a location, a distance, a parameter, a classification, or new geometry? Those results are not interchangeable. A successful closest-parameter calculation still requires evaluation before it becomes a spatial point.

PlaneSurface

6 members
#PlaneSurfacesurfaces

NexoNest explanation

A plane surface is a bounded surface portion, distinct from the infinite mathematical plane frame.

Domain and extents control evaluation. Converting it to Brep adds boundaries rather than making a solid.

Understand the underlying surface and the retained region

A parametric surface maps (u,v) to a spatial point. Local derivatives determine how a small UV step stretches or turns in 3D. A uniform parameter grid can therefore become very uneven spatially, especially near poles or degenerate parameter regions.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

Point

2 members
#Pointcoordinates

NexoNest explanation

Point is a GeometryBase object containing a location. Point3d is a numeric value type.

Use Point for geometry-object behavior and Point3d for calculations. Convert explicitly when moving between numeric coordinates and document geometry.

Distinguish locations, displacements, and frames

A coordinate triple only becomes meaningful with a frame and units. A point at (1,0,0) in a machine's local frame can occupy a different world position from the same numbers in WorldXY. Store the frame with exchanged coordinate data rather than relying on a document's current construction plane.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

Point3d.DistanceTo

def DistanceTo(self, other: Point3d) -> float

NexoNest explanation

Euclidean distance measures the straight segment between points, not travel along a curve or surface.

For distance along a path, use the curve's length methods. Coincident endpoints can have zero straight-line distance while the path between them has substantial length.

Choose the right notion of closeness

Straight-line distance, travel along a curve, and travel constrained to a surface answer different questions. Endpoints of a loop can coincide while traveling between them around the loop takes substantial length. Use the metric that matches the intended movement or clearance.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

Permanent link · Official RhinoCommon reference

Point3d.DistanceToSquared

def DistanceToSquared(self, other: Point3d) -> float

NexoNest explanation

Squared distance avoids a square root in comparisons. Compare it with a squared threshold.

A threshold of d model units becomes d*d in squared units. Nearest-point ordering is unchanged for finite nonnegative distances.

Rhino 8 Python example · geometry in memory

import Rhino.Geometry as rg
a, b = rg.Point3d(0, 0, 0), rg.Point3d(3, 4, 0)
assert a.DistanceToSquared(b) == 25.0
assert a.DistanceTo(b) == 5.0

Choose the right notion of closeness

Straight-line distance, travel along a curve, and travel constrained to a surface answer different questions. Endpoints of a loop can coincide while traveling between them around the loop takes substantial length. Use the metric that matches the intended movement or clearance.

Point3d.EpsilonEquals

def EpsilonEquals(self, other: Point3d, epsilon: float) -> bool

NexoNest explanation

Tolerance equality is not an exact identity and is generally not transitive.

A can be close to B and B close to C while A is not close to C. Use an explicit clustering policy when deduplicating points.

When to use this

Compare coordinate values within a chosen tolerance, while keeping a separate policy for grouping, hashing, and object identity.

Worked example · Nearness is not transitive

  1. Along one axis take A=0, B=0.75*epsilon, and C=1.5*epsilon.
  2. A is within epsilon of B, and B is within epsilon of C, but A is farther than epsilon from C.
  3. A clustering algorithm must choose whether chains count as one group or whether every point must stay close to a representative. A pairwise equality check does not make that choice.

Common mistakes

  • Using tolerance equality as though it were an exact equivalence relation.
  • Mixing coordinates or tolerance values from different unit systems.

Related lessons: #Point3d.DistanceTo · #Point3d.DistanceToSquared · #Point3d

A tolerance is a modeling policy, not a repair button

A distance tolerance has physical scale; an angular tolerance has a different unit and purpose. A 0.01 tolerance can mean ten millimeters in a meter-based dataset or a hundredth of a millimeter in a millimeter-based dataset. Choose it after unit conversion and according to the smallest feature that should remain distinct.

Point3d.Transform

def Transform(self, xform: Transform) -> None

NexoNest explanation

This method changes the point in place and returns None. Keep a copy if the original coordinates are needed.

Translation affects points because they represent positions. A pure translation leaves a direction vector unchanged.

Rhino 8 Python example · geometry in memory

import Rhino.Geometry as rg
p = rg.Point3d(1, 2, 3)
p.Transform(rg.Transform.Translation(10, 0, 0))
assert abs(p.X - 11) < 1e-9

Reason about transformation order with a known point

Transform composition is ordered. With RhinoCommon's point transformation convention, A*B applies B first and then A. Scaling x=1 by two and then translating by ten gives x=12; translating first and scaling afterward gives x=22.

API summary

Converts the string representation of a point to the equivalent Point3d structure.

Geometry behind this class

A point is a location, while a vector is a displacement. Coordinates use model units; subtracting two points produces a vector.

Distinguish locations, displacements, and frames

A coordinate triple only becomes meaningful with a frame and units. A point at (1,0,0) in a machine's local frame can occupy a different world position from the same numbers in WorldXY. Store the frame with exchanged coordinate data rather than relying on a document's current construction plane.

PointCloud

35 members
#PointClouddistancespatial-index

NexoNest explanation

A point cloud is a sample collection, not a connected surface.

Nearest-sample distance differs from distance to a reconstructed surface. Account for density, noise, and coordinate units.

Use an index to find candidates, then test geometry

A spatial index organizes inexpensive proxies such as points and bounding boxes. It reduces how many expensive geometry comparisons you need, but a proxy hit does not generally prove an exact intersection or a requested distance condition.

PointCloud.ClosestPoint

def ClosestPoint(self, testPoint: Point3d) -> int

NexoNest explanation

The result identifies the nearest stored sample, rather than projecting onto a surface between samples.

Check the index before accessing an item. Sparse regions can have large errors relative to an underlying physical shape.

Choose the right notion of closeness

Straight-line distance, travel along a curve, and travel constrained to a surface answer different questions. Endpoints of a loop can coincide while traveling between them around the loop takes substantial length. Use the metric that matches the intended movement or clearance.

PointCloudItem

9 members
#PointCloudItemcoordinates

NexoNest explanation

A point-cloud item exposes one sample and its optional attributes through the owning cloud.

Indices and associated data can change after insertions or removals. Copy values that must outlive edits.

Distinguish locations, displacements, and frames

A coordinate triple only becomes meaningful with a frame and units. A point at (1,0,0) in a machine's local frame can occupy a different world position from the same numbers in WorldXY. Store the frame with exchanged coordinate data rather than relying on a document's current construction plane.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

PolyCurve

17 members
#PolyCurvecurvestopology

NexoNest explanation

A polycurve joins curve segments into a composite. Global parameters differ from segment-local parameters.

Use mapping methods to transfer parameters. A joined sequence can retain gaps or discontinuities needing validation.

Separate a path's shape from its representation

A line, a circular arc, a polyline, and a NURBS curve can all be paths, but they encode shape differently. An exact analytic circle has angular evaluation; a Curve wrapper supplies a general parameter domain. Converting representation does not guarantee parameter identity.

Read the full concept lesson and practical checks →

PolyCurve.CleanUp

def CleanUp(self) -> Curve

API summary

Removes any nesting of polycurves. If this polycurve has just a single segment, the segment is returned. If, after nest removal, there are adjacent segments which are polylines, they are combined into a single polyline. The new curve may have a different domain from this polycurve. If the start and end segments of a closed input are polylines, the result may have a different seam location since the start and end segments will be combined.

PolyCurve.Explode

def Explode(self) -> Sequence[Curve]

NexoNest explanation

Exploding returns component curves with their own parameterizations and identities.

Keep original segment order when transferring attributes. A global polycurve parameter cannot be blindly reused on a component.

Connectivity is information beyond coordinates

Geometry describes shapes; topology records how pieces are connected and oriented. Two edges can have matching coordinates without being the same topological edge. A Brep combines surfaces with faces, loops, trims, edges, and vertices to represent these relationships.

Polyline.PointAt

def PointAt(self, t: float) -> Point3d

NexoNest explanation

Polyline parameters combine a segment index with a local segment fraction.

Segments of different lengths each occupy a parameter interval of length one. Use length-based sampling for uniform physical spacing.

Parameters are addresses, not distances

Think of C(t) as an address-to-position map. Its domain tells you which addresses are available; the derivative tells you how quickly position changes as the address changes. Changing the domain can change those numbers without changing the curve's shape.

PolylineCurve.CreateConvexHull2d

def CreateConvexHull2d(points: Iterable[Point2d]) -> tuple[PolylineCurve, Sequence[int]]

API summary

Attempts to create a closed PolylineCurve that is the anti-clockwise planar convex hull of the input points. In addition, the indices of the extremal points among the input points are returned in correct order. Possible duplicates among the input points are taken care of. The input pointsThe indices into the input points such that points[hullIndices[i]] = result[i]. Since the result is a closed polyline if successful, the start/end index is repeated at the beginning and end of the hullIndices. The closed PolylineCurve encompassing the input points, or null if the input points were either too few, or were found to be collinear.

Quaternion

43 members
#Quaternioninteroprotations

NexoNest explanation

A unit quaternion represents a rotation; q and -q represent the same rotation.

Normalize inputs when needed and maintain sign correspondence across sequences. Euler-angle singularities are avoided, but interpolation still needs a deliberate path convention.

Rotation representations have different ambiguities

Axis-angle, Euler angles, rotation matrices, and unit quaternions describe rotations with different conventions. A quaternion's four components are not four independent angles, and q and -q represent the same rotation.

Quaternion.Inverse

def Inverse(self) -> Quaternion

API summary

Computes a new inverted quaternion, (a/L2, -b/L2, -c/L2, -d/L2), where L2 = length squared = (a*a + b*b + c*c + d*d). This is the multiplicative inverse, i.e., (a,b,c,d)*(a/L2, -b/L2, -c/L2, -d/L2) = (1,0,0,0). If this is the zero quaternion, then the zero quaternion is returned.

Quaternion.GetRotation

GetRotation.Overloads[CLR signature](...)

NexoNest explanation

This output-only overload group requires explicit CLR selection in Rhino 8 Python.NET; a direct no-argument call is ambiguous.

Use Overloads to choose Plane, Transform, or angle-axis outputs. The selector avoids promising a direct call that fails at runtime.

Read Python.NET results in Python terms

A .NET out parameter is an output, not normally a Python argument. Python.NET collects outputs with the non-void return value in declaration order. A ref parameter still needs an initial input and also contributes its updated value to the result.

Axis-angle, Euler angles, rotation matrices, and unit quaternions describe rotations with different conventions. A quaternion's four components are not four independent angles, and q and -q represent the same rotation.

Ray3d

7 members
#Ray3dcurves

NexoNest explanation

A ray uses a position and direction. If the direction is not unit length, its parameter is not a distance.

Enforce the nonnegative parameter condition separately when modeling a physical ray. The evaluation equation can also produce points on its supporting line.

Separate a path's shape from its representation

A line, a circular arc, a polyline, and a NURBS curve can all be paths, but they encode shape differently. An exact analytic circle has angular evaluation; a Curve wrapper supplies a general parameter domain. Converting representation does not guarantee parameter identity.

Rectangle3d.CreateFromPolyline

def CreateFromPolyline(polyline: Iterable[Point3d]) -> Rectangle3d | tuple[Rectangle3d, float, float]

API summary

Attempts to create a rectangle from a polyline. This method only works well for polylines that already closely resemble rectangles. If the polyline contains more than four vertices, the least significant ones will be ignored. If the polylines is non-orthogonal, the discrepancies will be averaged away. This method should not be used as a Rectangle fitter.

Geometry behind this class

A rectangle uses a plane and two coordinate intervals. Orientation and interval direction affect evaluation.

Separate a path's shape from its representation

A line, a circular arc, a polyline, and a NURBS curve can all be paths, but they encode shape differently. An exact analytic circle has angular evaluation; a Curve wrapper supplies a general parameter domain. Converting representation does not guarantee parameter identity.
